title: Four Bowls, Still
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
A year after the charter passed, Toph broke another chair.

This one was ours.

“It was weak,” she said.

“You sat on the backrest,” Katara replied.

“Still weak.”

Aang examined the broken wood. “I can fix it.”

Three voices said, “No.”

He looked offended.

This was how I knew life was good.

Not perfect.

Good.

Cranefish Town had stopped calling itself a town sometime that spring. Too many people. Too many rail lines. Too much government. Someone proposed a new official name every month and none survived contact with the public.

Aang said names should grow naturally.

Toph said that was because he had no idea how committees worked.

I knew exactly how committees worked and therefore supported Aang.

The city kept changing.

So did we.

Katara split her time between the clinic and a new training program for healers and nonbender medics. She still overworked. Less often. When she did, we pointed it out and she became angry and then, irritatingly, listened.

Toph’s academy expanded into the lot next door. Mei became one of its most reliable administrators, which delighted me and horrified Toph because Mei had developed an appreciation for labeled shelves.

“I blame you,” Toph said.

“Organization is contagious.”

“Disease.”

Aang’s cultural school filled its blank shelf.

Not completely.

Never completely.

But enough that they needed another shelf for Things We Are Still Figuring Out.

Toph made the second plaque without being asked.

Aang did not tease her.

Much.

The Air Acolytes began taking more responsibility for the school, which meant Aang could travel without returning to seventeen decisions about sleeves.

He still received six.

Progress.

I left the council clerk’s office.

That surprised everyone, especially me.

Mara recruited me to help build an independent civic records bureau responsible for public access, conflict-of-interest disclosures, housing enforcement tracking, and emergency planning.

More responsibility.

Fewer people able to place lunch under my paperwork without passing three clerks and an extremely judgmental receptionist.

Toph approved.

Our house acquired scratches.

Good houses do.

The courtyard wall held.

The plum tree we thought was dead produced three blossoms in spring, then one tiny fruit that Aang guarded from birds with such intensity that a sparrow developed a personal feud with him.

Appa destroyed another gutter.

Momo stole an entire tray of dumplings during a policy dinner.

Katara blamed Aang.

Aang blamed structural incentives.

I blamed leaving dumplings near Momo.

Toph blamed society.

We did not have children.

Not then.

The conversation remained open.

Mei came to dinner twice a week anyway. Academy students slept in the courtyard after late training. Air Acolytes appeared asking impossible questions. Sokka visited and left inventions in places inventions should not be.

Family accumulated without asking permission from our categories.

On the anniversary of our first household agreement, Katara found the original paper in my locked file drawer.

“You kept it.”

“Of course I kept it.”

Toph leaned over the desk. “Read the stupid rules.”

We carried it to the kitchen.

The paper had softened at the folds. Toph’s inked thumbprint was still visible. Aang’s air swirl. Katara’s wave. The tiny filing cabinet Toph had drawn beside my name.

I read aloud.

Separate money.

Shared expenses.

Private rooms.

No reading correspondence.

No volunteering another person’s labor.

No turning the house into an official Avatar residence.

Sick people allowed to be sick without apologizing.

Help offered, not imposed.

Nobody’s fear of abandonment used to prevent another person from leaving.

We had broken some rules accidentally.

We had repaired them.

Others no longer fit exactly.

We revised.

Toph added: NO PUBLIC ASSEMBLIES IN THE COURTYARD WITHOUT UNANIMOUS CONSENT, underlined three times.

Aang accepted this with humility.

Katara added: REST IS NOT A REWARD FOR FINISHING EVERYTHING.

I objected that everything was never finished, which she claimed was the point.

Aang added: ASK BEFORE HELPING DOES NOT MEAN NEVER NOTICE.

Toph approved after changing “helping” to “interfering helpfully.”

I added: LOVE IS NOT A CONFLICT-OF-INTEREST DISCLOSURE.

Nobody understood what I meant.

I kept it.

Then Toph said, “We need a rule about chairs.”

Katara stared at the broken one.

“Don’t sit on the backrest.”

“Oppressive.”

“Use furniture as intended.”

“Authoritarian.”

Aang said, “What if we phrase it positively?”

Toph threw a napkin at him.

We ordered a new chair.

That evening, I cooked.

This was dangerous but legal.

Aang chopped vegetables until Katara took the knife away because he was airbending the scraps toward the compost bin and missing.

Toph sat on the counter giving instructions nobody requested.

Katara made sauce.

We ate at the table.

Four bowls.

Still.

The first time there had been four bowls, I had stared at them like they were a bridge I did not know how to cross.

Now one bowl had a chip from Toph dropping it. Aang’s had a badly painted sky bison on the side. Katara’s was deep enough for soup because she hated shallow dishes. Mine had a square pattern around the rim that Toph claimed she had not chosen on purpose.

Objects remembered.

So did people.

Aang stole a piece of fruit from Katara’s plate.

She slapped his fingers.

Toph stole one from Aang.

I stole one from Toph.

The table descended into lawlessness.

Eventually Katara restored order by threatening to remove dessert.

Aang called this an abuse of executive authority.

I told him to file an appeal.

Toph said she was the court.

“Absolutely not,” Katara and I said together.

After dinner, we climbed to the roof.

The city glowed below.

Aang sat with his legs hanging over the edge. Katara leaned against him. Toph sat cross-legged with both palms flat on the roof tiles, reading the house through vibration.

I lay back and looked at the stars.

“Do you ever think about forever?” Aang asked.

Toph groaned.

“Why would you do this to us?”

Katara smiled. “Sometimes.”

Aang looked at me.

I thought about the haphazard certainty I had once wanted from love.

Chosen forever.

Safe forever.

No jealousy. No fear. No leaving. No change.

Real love had been less clean and far more generous.

People got hurt.

People apologized badly, then better.

Duty interrupted dinner.

Anger survived forgiveness.

Home changed shape.

Nobody promised that choice made loss impossible.

“I think forever is too large to live in,” I said.

Aang considered that.

Toph nodded once.

Katara took my hand.

“So what do we live in?” she asked.

I looked at the roof beneath us.

Stone under Toph.

Water stored below for Katara.

Open sky over Aang.

My office light still on because I had forgotten to turn it off.

Of course.

“Today,” I said.

Toph made a face. “That was almost as bad as Twinkle Toes.”

Aang looked delighted.

“I liked it.”

“I know. That proves my point.”

Katara laughed.

I sat up.

Wind moved through Aang’s sleeves.

Somewhere below, water shifted in the pipes.

The house settled against its foundation.

The city carried on without asking whether our story had reached its ending.

Good.

I did not want an ending that turned us into certainty.

I wanted another breakfast.

Another argument.

Another meeting one of us forgot.

Another storm we hoped never came.

Another festival built from fragments.

Another night with four bowls on the table and no guarantee except that we would keep telling the truth while we were there.

Aang reached for my hand.

Katara reached for Toph’s.

Toph complained.

Nobody let go.

For the first time in my life, forever did not feel like a promise someone could break.

It felt like this:

Four people.

Four directions.

One imperfect home.

Chosen again in the morning.

The broken chair became a shelf.

Toph insisted this was practical rather than sentimental.

She bent the metal braces into clean supports while Aang sanded the wood and Katara complained about sawdust in the kitchen. I held pieces steady and contributed the essential skill of knowing when to stay out of Toph’s way.

We mounted it beside the front door.

On it went four things.

Aang placed a small wind chime from the cultural school.

Katara set down a blue glass bottle from the Southern Water Tribe.

Toph added the first four-pointed metal piece she had ever denied making for me.

I put our original household agreement beneath them in a wooden frame.

Toph groaned. “Paper as decoration. We’ve become terrible people.”

“You signed it.”

“I was young.”

“It was last year.”

“Ancient history.”

Aang stood behind us with his arms folded. “I like it.”

“Of course you do. You like feelings.”

“So do you.”

The room went silent.

Toph pointed at him. “Dangerous accusation.”

Katara kissed her cheek.

Toph complained for exactly three seconds before leaning into her.

That evening, four bowls sat on the table again.

Not because four had become sacred. People visited. People traveled. Sometimes one chair stayed empty for weeks. Sometimes the house filled with friends, students, healers, acolytes, council workers, and neighbors until privacy became a tactical objective.

Four simply meant tonight.

Aang told a terrible joke.

Katara laughed anyway.

Toph threw a piece of bread at him and missed on purpose.

I looked at them and felt no need to turn the moment into proof that forever existed.

Forever had frightened me when it sounded like a promise no human being could guarantee.

This was better.

Dinner tonight. A key in my pocket. A door I could close. A place at the table I could leave and return to. Three people who kept choosing me without pretending choice happened only once.

Tomorrow would ask again.

So would we.

bridge_outro: Four bowls still stood on the table when we returned from Riverstone Terrace's market. Aang had invited the neighbors; Katara had organized the food; Toph claimed she had only come because the chairs were less terrible than last time. Then Iroh arrived carrying tea, and Greg followed with a song he promised was short. I looked around the Lanternwell and understood that a shared world did not make anyone's obligations disappear. It made a second place to practice them honestly. Aang squeezed my shoulder, Katara saved the last dumpling for me, and Toph announced that our table was taking up entirely too much space. She moved her chair closer.
